subject: Private deployment: network runway & throughput targets (architecture review)
messages:
From: Sanjay Patel <sanjay@acmecorp.com>
To: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.ai>
Date: 2025-04-09T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private deployment: initial throughput request and network constraints

Camila — thanks again for the demo yesterday. We’re keen to move forward with a private VPC deployment of Redwood for LLM inference. Before we lock in capacity commitments, a few constraints from our infra team:

- We have two AZs in us-west-2; cross-AZ interconnect bandwidth is capped at 3 Gbps for customer-managed peering.
- On-prem side (data center B) has an uplink of 10 Gbps but an existing 40% baseline utilization during peak ETL windows.
- Desired SLA: 95th p99 latency target for short-lived request paths (~200 ms) and sustained throughput up to 35 QPS of medium-length (avg 150 tokens) generation workloads.

Can Redwood sketch expected GPU pool sizing and a recommended network topology that meets these goals while providing graceful degradation if cross-AZ peering saturates? Also: any suggested tests we should run pre-cutover to validate prefix/KV caching effectiveness?

Thanks —
Sanjay
Sanjay Patel
Head of AI Engineering, Acme Corp
From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.ai>
To: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>

Subject: Private deployment: initial throughput request and network constraints

Looping in Jonas and Lauren for sizing + network pattern guidance. Sanjay — thanks for the detail. Quick clarifying Qs before we propose numbers:

1) Is the 35 QPS steady for a 30-minute window or a sustained 24-hour plateau?
2) What percentage of requests are chat-style (multi-turn) vs single-shot generation? Multi-turns affect KV cache pressure and GPU memory footprint.
3) Are you expecting burst windows (x3-5) for traffic (e.g., batch launches)? If so, do you have an agreed burst budget or prefer staged throttle?

We’ve attached a starter capacity workbook and a recommended VPC sketch — Jonas, can you take a pass on sizing (GPU count, pod footprint, expected per-GPU sustained tokens/sec with 16-bit and 8-bit quant profiles) and call out network egress breakpoints?

Action: I’ll coordinate a short runbook for pre-cutover tests (bandwidth soak, cache-warmup, tail-latency ramps).

—
Camila Reyes

Subject: Re: Private deployment: initial throughput request and network constraints

Camila / Lauren — I ran a quick modeling pass based on Sanjay’s inputs and two workload profiles (A: chat-heavy multi-turn; B: single-shot generation). Key assumptions: avg request size 150 tokens, generation length 60 tokens; medium model family (7B-13B) quantized to 8-bit for cost-sensitive sustained throughput.

Sizing proposal (conservative headroom for 95th p99 latency at ~200 ms):
- Baseline (steady 35 QPS sustained): 6 GPU nodes (each node: 8x A100-style vGPUs equivalent in our runtime packing) — expected sustained throughput ~6 QPS per physical GPU-equivalent at 8-bit for the model profile.
- Burst-capable (3x short bursts to 105 QPS for up to 10 min): add 2 hot standby nodes (warm pool) + leverage queue-based admission control; expected warmup for KV cache ~90–120s to reach optimal hit rates.
- Headroom and failover: reserve a lightweight fallback model variant (quant 4-bit / distilled) on an extra 1–2 nodes to keep token throughput during severe bandwidth or GPU contention.

Network implications:
- Cross-AZ peering at 3 Gbps becomes the limiting factor for multi-AZ synchronous calls. Our estimate: at 35 QPS and avg 210 tokens/request (total request + response), token egress (sustained) ~ 35 * 210 * 1 token ~= ~7.35k tokens/sec — translate to ~0.8–1.2 Gbps depending on serialization. That fits under 3 Gbps but leaves limited headroom for bursts and other egress (metrics, logs, artifacts).
- Recommend asymmetrical routing: place primary inference pool in the AZ with the majority traffic and use cross-AZ peering only for failover; keep synchronous cross-AZ calls to a minimum. If Acme requires active-active across both AZs, we should plan for dedicated interconnect or increase peering to >=6 Gbps.

Operational notes and tests to run:
- Bandwidth soak: sustained transfer of synthetic payloads at expected tokens/sec for 30 min, observe tail latencies and cross-AZ packet drops.
- Cache-warmup trial: replay 10k representative requests to measure KV hit rate and latency reduction (track warmup curve).
- Egress noise test: run normal infra metrics/log shipping concurrently to measure available headroom.

I’ve attached a small CSV with microbenchmarks from a similar footprint: bandwidth_test_results_20250408.csv. Lauren — can you validate the p99 latency math and decide whether the 2 hot nodes are sufficient given Acme’s SLA?

-Jonas
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Camila Reyes <camila.reyes@redwood.ai>
To: Sanjay Patel <sanjay@acmecorp.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.ai>, Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>, infraops@acmecorp.com
Date: 2025-04-11T15:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment: initial throughput request and network constraints

Sanjay — summary and next steps based on the sizing pass above:

Summary (what we recommend)
- Sizing: initial private GPU pool = 6 production GPUs + 2 warm standby GPUs + 1 fallback-model GPU (total logical footprint: 9 nodes). This provides ~30–40% headroom for the steady 35 QPS target and capacity for short bursts using the warm pool.
- Network: prefer single-AZ primary with cross-AZ peering used for failover. If you need active-active across AZs, request increased peering to >=6 Gbps or a dedicated private interconnect.
- Cache & latency: KV cache warmups require ~2 minutes to reach effective hit rates for multi-turn chat; recommend a cache-warmup window during deploy and a steady-state warm pool strategy for peak hours.

Pre-cutover test plan (we’ll collaborate on execution)
1) Bandwidth soak (30 min) at 110% of expected sustained tokens/sec while capturing p50/p95/p99 latency.
2) Cache-warmup replay (10k requests) to measure hit-rate curve and tail reduction.
3) Controlled burst: 3x traffic for 10 minutes to validate warm pool scaling and admission control fallback to distilled model.
4) Egress/metrics noise test: run standard logging and metrics to ensure <20% of peering used by non-inference traffic during peak.

Deliverables we’ll share by EOD tomorrow:
- Updated capacity workbook with cost and runbook: privgpu_capacity_workbook_v1.xlsx (rev A).
- Network sketch with routing options: acme_vpc_vlan_topology.drawio.
- Bandwidth microbenchmarks we ran: bandwidth_test_results_20250408.csv.

Can we schedule a 30-min runbook walk-through this week? I’m free Thu 10–12 PDT or Fri 14–17 PDT.

Thanks — looking forward to the cutover plan.

—
Camila Reyes
Solutions Architect, Redwood Inference
